claims.text: Phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is governed by competition between the thermodynamic driving force for Al-induced ordering and kinetic hindrance from sluggish multicomponent diffusion.
At high temperature, Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 forms a homogeneous BCC state.
High atomic mobility at high temperature keeps the alloy's free energy spatially uniform.
Cooling below a critical temperature increases an Al-driven free-energy imbalance that promotes nucleation of an ordered B2 or L12 phase.
Kinetic barriers associated with multicomponent diffusion delay the ordering transformation.
Homogenization at approximately 1200°C produces a single-phase BCC state in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
Quenching from 1200°C freezes the BCC state as a room-temperature metastable state.
Samples will be annealed at approximately 850°C under argon for durations ranging from 1 to 100 hours.
Subcritical annealing causes Al partitioning and short-range chemical ordering within the BCC matrix.
Al partitioning and short-range order lead to nucleation and growth of ordered B2 or L12 intermetallic precipitates.
High Al content lowers the free energy of an ordered B2 or L12 structure relative to disordered BCC below a critical temperature.
Atomic diffusion in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is inherently sluggish.
Sufficient annealing time below the critical temperature permits the thermodynamic driving force to overcome resistance to atomic migration.
At 850°C, the BCC phase will gradually transform into an ordered phase.
The transformation will produce ordered-phase XRD peaks and nanoscale precipitates visible by TEM.
The ordered-phase fraction will increase with annealing duration.
The ordered transformation occurs only below a critical temperature and after sufficient annealing time.
At higher temperatures, the BCC state is thermodynamically stable and the ordered phase will not form.
Short annealing durations will not permit formation of the ordered phase because of the kinetic barrier.
Failure to observe ordered-phase peaks or precipitates at or below 850°C after prolonged annealing, or failure to observe time-dependent evolution, would falsify the hypothesis.
